drivingQuestion: Why does the mishna state the Torah-level cases after the rabbinic ones?
outcomeNote: redundancy explained as a stylistic ordering

segments.he: לֹא עוֹלִין בָּאִילָן וְלֹא רוֹכְבִין עַל גַּבֵּי בְּהֵמָה וְכוּ׳. הַשְׁתָּא דְּרַבָּנַן אָמְרַתְּ לָא, דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא מִיבַּעְיָא?! זוֹ וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר זוֹ קָתָנֵי.
segments.en: § The mishna taught: One may not pass the Shabbat limit for it, i.e., to go and hear it, nor may one clear a pile of rubble to uncover a buried shofar. «One may not climb a tree, nor may one ride on an animal» to find a shofar to sound. The Gemara questions the order of these prohibitions: «Now» that «you have said» that to sound the shofar one «may not» perform an action that is prohibited «by rabbinic law,» i.e., passing the Shabbat limit or clearing a pile of rubble, «is» it «necessary» to say that one may not perform an action that could lead to an act prohibited «by Torah law,» i.e., climbing a tree or riding an animal? The Gemara answers: The mishna «teaches» employing the style: «This, and it is unnecessary to say that.» It begins with the more novel case before moving on to the more straightforward one.

moves.about: having ruled out rabbinic prohibitions, the Torah-level cases are superfluous
